definition: A model of three overlapping ways to understand and teach student writing: study skills (writing as a transferable individual skill), academic socialisation (learning a discipline's stable discourses and genres) and academic literacies (writing as social practice bound up with meaning making, identity, power and what counts as knowledge in an institution). Reach for it to diagnose the assumptions behind writing support, to design teaching that makes genre and mode shifts explicit without treating students as deficient, and to engage staff as writers. It is not a teaching method with steps: its authors offer it as a design frame, and critics say its pedagogy is unclear.
extendedDefinition: Mary Lea and Brian Street proposed the three models in a study of student writing in UK universities (*Studies in Higher Education*, 1998) and restated them, with two worked applications, in *Theory Into Practice* (2006) [D:LS2006, p. 368; D:LS1998, not read]. The study skills model treats writing as an individual, cognitive skill; academic socialisation treats it as acculturation into a discipline's discourses and genres; academic literacies treats it as social practice involving meaning making, identity, power and authority; it asks what counts as knowledge in each context [D:LS2006, pp. 368-369]. The authors say the models overlap and are not mutually exclusive, and that the first two have guided most curriculum and research [D:LS2006, p. 369]. Its main use is as a frame for writing development and course design that challenges a deficit view of students [D:LS2006, pp. 368, 376]. Its disputes: whether the models are a hierarchy or nested, and whether academic literacies yields a workable pedagogy [D:DW2024].

definition: Wingate's case for teaching academic literacy inside every discipline's curriculum, through collaboration between EAP or learning development specialists and subject lecturers, using genre analysis of student texts, six ways to embed it in ordinary teaching and staff development for lecturers. Reach for it to design or argue for embedded academic literacy provision, to plan collaboration between a library or skills team and a department, or to critique generic study skills provision. It is not a theory of what literacy is: for that, use Lea and Street's academic literacies model.
extendedDefinition: Ursula Wingate, of King's College London, set out in a 2015 plenary, published in 2016 and 2018, that academic literacy, the ability to communicate competently in a discipline's discourse community, must be taught to all students within the curriculum [D:WG2018, pp. 349-350]. She argues that the dominant provision, generic EAP and study skills courses outside the disciplines, is remedial, rests on misconceptions of students' needs and misallocates responsibility away from subject lecturers [D:WG2018, pp. 350-351]. She reports a genre-based writing intervention built with subject lecturers, a PGCAP module that taught six ways to embed literacy in teaching, and the Australian curriculum-integrated model [D:WG2018, pp. 353-361]. She concludes that effective support needs three things: curriculum embedding, genre analysis and collaboration between EAP and subject specialists [D:WG2018, p. 362]. Her own limits: the intervention was additional rather than embedded, collaboration was hard to sustain and no performance data was gathered [D:WG2018, p. 358].

definition: A behavioural therapy that aims to increase psychological flexibility: making room for difficult thoughts and feelings rather than fighting them, and acting on chosen values. Reach for it to describe or explain the ACT model, its six processes and its tools. Not for choosing anyone's treatment, and not as a self-help programme in itself.
extendedDefinition: Developed by Steven Hayes, Kirk Strosahl and Kelly Wilson (first book 1999; second edition 2012), ACT is one of the third-wave behaviour therapies [D:CUL2008]. It rests on functional contextualism and relational frame theory, a behavioural account of language and cognition [D:HAY2006]. Its aim is psychological flexibility: contacting the present moment fully and changing or persisting in behaviour when that serves one's values. Six linked processes build it: acceptance, cognitive defusion, contact with the present moment, self as context, values and committed action [D:HAY2006; D:ZHA2018]. A review of 20 meta-analyses found it efficacious for anxiety, depression, substance use, pain and mixed groups, though not consistently better than CBT [D:GLO2020]. The main dispute is how strong that evidence is: a stricter meta-analysis judged it not yet well established for any disorder [D:OST2014]. NICE names it, with CBT, among the psychological therapies for chronic primary pain [D:NICE2021].
